What this is about A calculator computes exactly what you are typing in at the moment. If you want the same calculation for twenty prices, you type it twenty times, and each time a typo can happen. A program, on the other hand, computes what you have written down for it once as often as you like, with as many numbers as you like and without new typos, once it is correct. This chapter explores how to write down such a list of instructions for a computer and how to get the computer to carry it out. By the end, Python runs on your own computer, on Windows or on Linux. You can use it to calculate, write and start small programs, and you can read the messages with which Python points out errors. How to work with this chapter. A computer does only what it is told to do, step by step. This section explains what a program is, which instructions the processor of a computer understands, and why programs are written down in a language of their own. The program A computer can calculate very fast, but it decides nothing on its own. Before it does anything useful, someone has to tell it exactly which steps to carry out and in which order. A recipe. A cooking recipe is such a sequence of steps “Bring water to a boil. Add the pasta. Wait nine minutes. Drain.” Whoever follows it does not need to know why pasta needs nine minutes. They only need to understand each step unambiguously and keep to the order. Knowing what something is, and knowing how to find it. The sentence “The square root of 2 is the positive number that, multiplied by itself, gives 2” describes completely. But it does not say how to find this number. A recipe that delivers the number step by step is knowledge of a different kind it describes a method. A computer can only do something with knowledge of this second kind. A program is a sequence of unambiguously described steps that a computer carries out one after another, without asking questions. A single step of a program is called a statement . What the processor understands machine instructions In a computer, the steps of a program are carried out by the processor , a chip that calculates and controls the sequence of steps. Its instructions are much simpler than “form the mean of and ”. A very literal worker. You can picture the processor as an extremely fast worker with a tiny vocabulary. It understands instructions such as “fetch the number from memory cell 12”, “add two numbers”, “divide two numbers” or “continue at instruction 3”. It cannot do more than that, but it manages billions of these every second. The picture is only an aid to imagination; the processor understands nothing in the human sense, but carries out its instructions mechanically. A machine instruction is an instruction that the processor can carry out directly. It is stored in memory as a number; from this number the processor recognizes what to do. A program that consists only of machine instructions is called machine code . Step 2 of Heron's recipe breaks down into machine instructions roughly like this Fetch the number from memory. Divide 2 by this number. Add to the result. Divide the result by 2. Store the result in memory as the new . Each of these instructions is a number in memory. Which number means which instruction is defined differently for each family of processors. The processors of most PCs understand different numbers than those of a smartphone. Machine code for one therefore does not run on the other. ⁠ In short The processor understands only very simple machine instructions, which are stored as numbers in memory, and each processor family has its own. Every machine instruction is permanently built into the processor chip. One part of the processor, the arithmetic unit, adds two numbers, for example. Another part, the control unit, reads the number of the next instruction and connects the matching parts with each other, such as “memory cell 12 to the input of the arithmetic unit, result back to memory”. The fewer and simpler the instructions, the smaller, faster and more economical the chip can be built. Everything complicated arises from many simple instructions running one after another, just as you can build a whole castle from a few kinds of Lego bricks. The processor always runs through the same cycle fetch the instruction, decode the instruction, execute the instruction, move on to the next instruction. The programming language Machine code is a long sequence of numbers. People can hardly read it, and it applies to only one processor family. A recipe in everyday language would be more convenient, but everyday language is ambiguous. Ambiguity. “I saw the man with the binoculars.” Did I have the binoculars, or did the man? A person guesses the intended meaning from the context. A computer cannot do that; it needs exactly one meaning for every sentence. A programming language is an artificial language in which it is precisely defined which texts are allowed and what each allowed text does. Python, C and C++ are programming languages. In Python, you write the first pass of Heron's recipe with like this The character / means “divided by”, + means “plus”, and the parentheses work as in mathematics. In Python, this line has exactly one meaning divide 2 by 1, add 1, divide the result by 2. ⁠ In short A programming language is an artificial language without ambiguity in which programs are written down. Syntax With a programming language, two questions have to be kept apart Is a text allowed at all? And what does it do? The first question concerns only the form. Form without meaning. The sentence “The wulp blinks the graffel.” is grammatically well built subject, verb, object. It just means nothing. “Graffel the blinks wulp the.”, on the other hand, is wrong even in its form. Whether a sentence is well built can be checked without knowing its meaning. The syntax of a programming language is the set of all rules that determine which texts are allowed in it. In Python, 1 + 2 / 1 / 2 is allowed. The following lines violate the syntax 1 + 2 / 1 / 2 A parenthesis is opened and never closed. 1 + / 2 A number is missing between + and / . ⁠ In short The syntax determines the allowed form, regardless of what a text means. Semantics A text in an allowed form must also have a defined effect. The semantics of a programming language determines what an allowed text means, that is, what happens when it is run. The line 7 / 2 is allowed in Python and in C, so it has the correct form in both languages. In Python it means “divide 7 by 2”, and the result is 3.5. In C, with whole numbers, the same text means “divide and drop the remainder”, and the result is 3. Same form, different meaning. A second example if you want to compute the mean of 3 and 4 and write 3 + 4 / 2 , you have written an allowed text. But its defined meaning is , not the intended mean . The semantics follows the text, not the intention. ⁠ In short The semantics determines what an allowed text does. The syntax of Python is written down as a formal grammar a list of rules such as “an expression in parentheses is an opening parenthesis, then an expression, then a closing parenthesis”. It is given in full in the Python Language Reference. The program that runs Python texts contains a part that is generated from exactly this grammar and checks every text against its rules. The semantics, by contrast, is described in words for every allowed form, the language reference says what it does. Source code What a person writes down in a programming language needs a name to distinguish it from machine code. The source code of a program is its text in a programming language, the way people write and read it. The line 1 + 2 / 1 / 2 is a very short piece of Python source code. A processor cannot run it, because it understands only machine instructions. So something has to translate between the source code and the processor. ⁠ In short Source code is the program in the form in which people write it; the processor cannot run it directly. The processor understands only machine code; people write source code. This section shows the two basic ways of closing this gap, and which way Python takes. The compiler Source code has to be translated into machine code. A program can take on this job. A book translator. A book is translated completely once, then printed and sold. The readers of the translation no longer need the translator; they hold a finished book in their hands. A compiler is a program that translates a source code completely into machine code before that code is run. The result is saved as a separate file that runs without the compiler. Such a file is called an executable file . On Windows, its name usually ends in .exe . Programs in the C language are translated this way. From the source code hallo.c , the compiler gcc produces the executable file hallo.exe Windows or hallo Linux . You then start this file directly, as often as you like and without the compiler. It contains machine code for a particular processor family and a particular operating system; for a different computer, you have to translate again. ⁠ In short A compiler translates the whole source code once, in advance, into an executable file of machine code. The interpreter It also works without an executable file a program can read the source code and itself do what it says. A human interpreter. In a conversation between two languages, an interpreter sits in and translates while people are speaking. No written result is produced; at the next conversation, the interpreter has to be there again. The picture captures the role of an interpreter program, not every detail of how it works. An interpreter is a program that reads a source code and itself carries out the steps described in it. It produces no executable file and therefore has to be present every time the program is started. Python programs run this way. You start the source code hallo.py with a command such as python hallo.py . The program python is the interpreter it reads the file and carries out what it says. All the while, the processor runs the machine code of the interpreter, never the Python source code itself. The two ways compared | | Compiler | Interpreter | | | | | | translation happens | once, before any start | at every start | | result | executable file | no file, only the effect | | what you pass on | the executable file | the source code; the recipient needs the interpreter | | runs on | the processor family and the operating system it was translated for | any computer for which the interpreter exists | | speed | fast | slower, because the interpreter does work at every step | ⁠ In short An interpreter runs the source code itself, without producing an executable file. An interpreter has two advantages that are decisive for Python. You can type in a line and immediately see what it does, without a translation step in between. And the same source code runs unchanged on Windows, Linux and macOS, on the processor of a PC as well as on the completely different processor of a newer Mac; only the interpreter itself has to exist for each system. The price is speed. At every step, the interpreter first has to do work of its own before the actual calculation happens. Computation heavy programs are therefore often written so that the heavy parts run in ready made, translated machine code that Python merely calls. Python and CPython The word “Python” refers to two different things a language and a program. Python is a programming language; its syntax and semantics are laid down in the Python Language Reference. CPython is the program that runs Python source code and is offered on python.org ; it is itself written in the C language. CPython is the original and by far the most widely used program of this kind. New language features usually appear there first. There are other programs that run Python source code, for example PyPy, which runs many programs faster. They follow the same language reference, that is, the same syntax and semantics. In this series, the program python always means CPython. ⁠ In short Python is the language; CPython is the program that runs it. Bytecode CPython is an interpreter, but it does not read the source code line by line like a human interpreter. It works in two phases. A cook with index cards. A cook first reads through the whole recipe and writes each step on index cards in their own shorthand. If they come across an illegible sentence while doing so, they do not even start. Only when all the cards are finished do they work through them in order. A picture; what the “cards” and the “shorthand” are in CPython follows now. Bytecode is a sequence of simple instructions into which CPython translates the entire source code before it begins running it. The instructions are designed for an imaginary machine, not for a real processor. A part of CPython then works through the bytecode instruction by instruction the interpreter loop . So a Python program runs like this Figure 2 abb 2 , left ⁠ Translate. CPython reads the whole file, checks its syntax and generates bytecode from it. Nothing is run yet. ⁠ Run. The interpreter loop takes one bytecode instruction after another. For each instruction, the processor runs a piece of machine code that is part of CPython and implements exactly this instruction. For a program that you start, CPython creates the bytecode only in main memory. No executable file is produced. The picture of the human interpreter from Subsection 2.2 stufe 2 2 is therefore only half right CPython first translates the whole file and then runs it. Two ways from source code to execution. Left, Python the program python CPython translates the whole file into bytecode at every start and then works through it in its interpreter loop. Right, C the compiler translates once in advance into an executable file, which the processor then runs without the compiler. The line 1 + 2 / 1 / 2 gives rise to bytecode instructions such as “provide the number 1”, “divide”, “add”. The translator even goes one step further an expression that consists only of fixed numbers is already computed during translation. The bytecode then contains the number 1.5 directly, and there is nothing left to compute when it runs. What the bytecode looks like exactly depends on the Python version; it is an internal tool of CPython and can change with every new version. One consequence of the two phases matters in practice if any part of the file violates the syntax, no bytecode is produced at all. Then not a single line runs, not even the first. ⁠ In short CPython first translates the whole file into bytecode and then runs this bytecode instruction by instruction. Splitting up a text and checking its syntax takes a lot of work. If CPython read the text anew at every step, it would have to split up the same line a thousand times when it is run a thousand times. With bytecode, the splitting up happens once at the beginning. After that, the bytecode instructions are simple and uniform, and the interpreter loop can recognize and run each of them quickly. In addition, the bytecode is the same on all processors. Only CPython itself has to be translated once with a compiler for each processor family and each operating system; after that, it runs the same bytecode everywhere. That is why Python is said to be interpreted, even though it contains a small translator. For Python, the line between “compiled” and “interpreted” is blurred. At its core, the interpreter loop is a single loop in the C source code of CPython fetch the next bytecode instruction, look up which instruction it is, run the matching piece of machine code, start over. This is the same cycle that the processor runs through with its machine instructions fetch, decode, execute Subsection 1.2 programme und programmiersprachen.html stufe 1 2 . That is why one speaks of an imaginary or virtual machine in software, CPython plays a processor whose instructions are the bytecode. Python can be used like a calculator you type in a line and immediately see the result. This section shows this way of working and the first building blocks of Python values, expressions, strings and calling a function. Interactive mode To try out a single line, you do not want to create a file. Python offers a way of working of its own for this. A calculator. On a calculator, you type a calculation, press “=” and read off the result. Then you type the next calculation. Python works exactly like this when you start it without a file name. In interactive mode , Python reads an input, runs it, displays the result and then waits for the next input. The prompt of the interactive mode is . This cycle of reading, running and displaying is called the read–eval–print loop , REPL for short. In the terminal, start py Windows or python3 Linux without anything after it. Python reports its version and waits for input After each , type a line and press Enter. Python answers on the next line and shows again. A few useful moves ⁠ Exiting type exit from Python 3.13 on; exit with parentheses works in every version , or press Ctrl+D on Linux, Ctrl+Z and then Enter on Windows. After that, the prompt of the terminal appears again. ⁠ Earlier inputs The up arrow key brings back the last input; you can change it and send it again with Enter. ⁠ Incomplete input If something is still missing, such as a closing parenthesis, Python shows ... instead of and waits for the rest of the input. From Python 3.13 on, the interactive mode is in color; in this chapter, the sessions are printed without colors. ⁠ In short In interactive mode, you type a line after , and Python answers immediately. The name read–eval–print loop comes from the programming language Lisp. In the 1960s, Lisp systems already had exactly this cycle read an input read , compute it evaluate , output the result print , start over loop . Many languages have adopted it because it lets you try out a language without writing a whole program. Since Python 3.13, CPython has come with a revised interactive mode the prompt and the error messages are in color, you can edit multi line inputs as a whole, exit and help work without parentheses, and the keys F1, F2 and F3 open the help, the history and a mode for pasting longer texts. From Python 3.14 on, it also colors the typed lines according to their syntax. In older versions and in some environments, the simpler earlier version appears; what it computes is the same. The value A calculator works with numbers. Python, too, needs a name for the data it works with. A value is a single piece of data that Python works with, for example the number 42 or the number 0.5. In Python, numbers with decimal places are written with a point, not with a comma 0.5 , not 0,5. In this chapter, numbers in running text also use a decimal point, just as in Python lines and in the answers from Python. If you type in a number, the interactive mode shows its value. It writes the value the way Python itself would write it and, for example, leaves out a superfluous zero at the end ⁠ In short A value is a piece of data such as the number 42; in Python, decimal places come after a point. The expression Usually, you do not type in a finished value but a calculation whose value Python has yet to determine. An expression is a piece of source code that Python can compute to a value. Computing the value of an expression is called evaluation . 2 + 3 is an expression with the value 5. A single number such as 42 is also an expression, the simplest one of all its value is the number itself. The interactive mode evaluates every expression you type in and displays the value on the next line. So the sessions above are nothing but pairs of expression and value. ⁠ In short An expression is source code that yields a value; the interactive mode displays this value immediately. Calculating as on a calculator Python has its own symbols for the basic arithmetic operations and for powers. | Symbol | Meaning | Example | Value | | | | | | | + | plus | 7 + 2 | 9 | | | minus | 7 2 | 5 | | | times | 7 2 | 14 | | / | divided by | 7 / 2 | 3.5 | | | to the power of | 2 10 | 1024 | Rules. Python calculates as in mathematics powers before multiplication and division, multiplication and division before addition and subtraction. 100 + 220 2 gives 540; if you want to add first, you use parentheses 100 + 220 2 gives 640. Only round parentheses group a calculation. Square brackets and curly braces have other meanings in Python. Spaces around the operators are allowed but not necessary; they make a line easier to read. Python always writes the result of / with a point, even when the division comes out even 12 / 4 gives 3.0 . Powers of ten are written with e 2.5e 3 means , that is, 2.5 g if the number is a weight in kilograms. Likewise, 4.7e3 is the number 4700. Python displays results with decimal places with up to 17 significant digits. How many of them are meaningful is up to you when you read off the result. Python knows no units. You have to keep track of the unit of a number in your head. First A 450 g jar of chocolate spread costs €4.49. What does one kilogram cost? You divide the price by the weight in kilograms, that is, by 0.45. Second €1000 sits in a savings account for ten years at 2 % interest per year. The interest stays in the account and earns interest itself in the following year. So every year, the balance is multiplied by 1.02, and after ten years by in total. Third A sheet of printer paper is about 0.1 mm thick, that is , in Python 1e 4 . How high is a pack of 500 sheets? In the second line, Python first computes the power 1.02 10 and then multiplies it by 1000, powers before multiplication. Read off the kilogram costs about €9.98, after ten years there is about €1219 in the account, and the pack is 0.05 m, that is, 5 cm high. The last result. The interactive mode remembers the last displayed value under the symbol underscore , like the ANS key of a calculator. After the session above, 100 therefore gives 5.0 , the height of the pack in centimeters. This works only in interactive mode. Careful with the comma. If you are used to a decimal comma and type 2,5 2 instead of 2.5 2 out of habit, you get no error message but a wrong result Python reads the comma as a separator between two values 2 and 5 2 . It displays both in parentheses instead of computing 5.0. ⁠ In short Python calculates with + / and round parentheses according to the rules of mathematics; decimal places come after a point, and it knows no units. For “to the power of”, no single symbol has become established in programming languages. Python follows the notation , which the language Fortran already used in the 1950s. The symbol ^ , on the other hand, Python took over from the language C, where it means an operation on individual binary digits that has nothing to do with powers. That is why 2 ^ 3 gives 1 in Python and not 8, and it does so without an error message. If you are used to the symbol ^ from spreadsheets or calculators, watch out for this. The recipe in interactive mode first by hand, then ready made With what has been explained so far, you can run Heron's recipe from Subsection 1.1 programme und programmiersprachen.html stufe 1 1 in interactive mode first by hand, pass by pass, then with the ready made way that comes with Python. By hand. The first pass with is 1 + 2/1 / 2 . For every further pass, you need the last result as the new ; stands for it. With the up arrow key, you bring back the line + 2/ / 2 and send it again After the fifth pass, nothing changes anymore the recipe has reached its goal. Ready made. The square root is the power with the exponent . Python can therefore compute it without a recipe Comparison. Both ways agree in the first 15 decimal places | Way | Result | | | | | Heron by hand, from the 5th pass on | 1.414213562373095 | | ready made with 2 0.5 | 1.4142135623730951 | | true value | | The difference in the 16th decimal place has a simple cause Python does not calculate with infinitely many digits but rounds every intermediate result to a fixed number of digits. Between two neighboring rounded numbers, there is therefore a smallest step. The recipe rounds several times in each pass and in the end stays one such step away from the built in result. Here the ready made way lies closer to the true value and needs no passes and no starting estimate; that is why you use it whenever it exists. By hand, every pass had to be sent off individually. Taking exactly such repetitions off your hands is what a program is for. ⁠ In short Heron's recipe runs in interactive mode pass by pass and, after five passes, arrives at the built in result of 2 0.5 except for the last digit. Text as a value the string Programs output not only numbers but also text, such as “Price in euros ” before a result. Text must therefore be able to be a value, too. A string is a value that consists of text. In source code, it stands between two straight quotation marks, "Hallo" , or between two apostrophes, 'Hallo' . Three inputs in interactive mode The interactive mode displays a string with apostrophes, even if you typed it with quotation marks; both mean the same. The second line is more important "7 6" is not computed. Between quotation marks, 7 6 is just a sequence of five characters. The quotation marks must be the straight ones from the keyboard. The typographic curly quotes from a word processor, “ and ” in English or „ and “ in German, are different characters for Python. ⁠ In short Text in straight quotation marks is a string, that is, a value that Python does not calculate with. The interactive mode displays every value the way you would write it in source code. That is why '7 6' appears there with apostrophes and 42 without you can see at once whether the result is a number or a text. Without this marking, the number 42 and the text made of the characters “4” and “2” could not be told apart on the screen. The function Many tasks occur in almost every program, for example writing something on the screen. For these, Python comes with ready made subprograms. A key on the calculator. The key of a calculator triggers a small built in program. You do not need to know how it calculates; you put a number in and get the square root out. A function is a ready made subprogram with a name that you can have run when needed. Python comes with the function named print . It writes values as text to the terminal. ⁠ In short A function is a ready made subprogram with a name. The function call print A function does something only when you have it run. There is a fixed notation for this. A function call has a function run. You write its name, followed by round parentheses, and inside the parentheses the values that the function is to work with, separated by commas. The function print writes the values in its parentheses on one line, separated by one space each. Strings appear without quotation marks. If there is an expression in the parentheses, Python evaluates it first and then outputs its value. A call without values, print , writes an empty line. In interactive mode, "Hallo" and print "Hallo" look similar but are different. In the first case, the interactive mode displays the value of an expression, with apostrophes. In the second case, the function print itself writes the text to the terminal, without apostrophes. Afterwards, the call of print has no value that the interactive mode would still display. ⁠ In short You call a function with its name and round parentheses; print writes the values in the parentheses to the terminal. Whatever you type in interactive mode is lost when you exit. This section shows how to save a program in a file, which tool you use to write this file and how to run it. The editor Saving a program in a file requires a program with which you write and save plain text without anything being added. Plain text. A program file may contain only the characters you type. A word processor such as Word, on the other hand, also saves fonts, page margins and paragraph formats, and while you type, it replaces straight quotation marks with typographic ones. Python, however, does not recognize typographic quotation marks as the beginning or end of a string. A word processor is therefore unsuitable for programs. An editor is a program with which you write and save plain text files. An editor for programmers also helps you write source code it colors the code according to its syntax, marks violations of the syntax while you type and can run a program at the push of a button. ⁠ Visual Studio Code VS Code for short is a free editor for Windows and Linux, which you can get at code.visualstudio.com . On Ubuntu, you can alternatively install it with sudo snap install classic code . After the first start, install the “Python” extension from Microsoft via the Extensions icon on the left edge. It provides the coloring, the error marking and the button for running a program; it does not contain Python itself. ⁠ IDLE is a simple editor that is part of Python. On Windows, the Python install manager creates the entry “IDLE Python 3.14 ” in the Start menu, matching the installed version. On Ubuntu, you install it with sudo apt install idle and start it with the command idle . You begin a new program with “File”, “New File”. For the programs in this chapter, create a folder python kurs in your home folder and save all files there. In VS Code, you open this folder with “File”, “Open Folder”; you then create new files in it. On Windows, File Explorer often hides file name extensions. Turn them on “View”, “Show”, “File name extensions” so that you can see whether a file is really called hallo.py and not hallo.py.txt . ⁠ In short You write programs with an editor that saves plain text, ideally with an editor for programmers such as VS Code or IDLE. While you type, an editor for programmers constantly reads the source code along and splits it up the same way the translator of CPython does in its first phase Subsection 2.4 vom quelltext zur ausfuhrung compiler und interpreter.html stufe 2 4 into numbers, operators, parentheses, strings and names. Each kind of component gets its own color; a string that is never closed therefore visibly colors the rest of the line as well. Then the editor checks the components against the grammar of the language and underlines every place where the grammar is violated. This check is the same kind of check that CPython performs before running a program; the editor merely does it earlier, namely while you are writing. What will happen when the program runs, on the other hand, it cannot fully foresee. The script With an editor, you can write the source code of a program into a file and run it as often as you like. A script is a text file with Python source code whose name ends in .py . Python runs a script by translating the file and then running each of its lines once, from top to bottom. Preparing the folder. Two commands are enough, and they are the same on Windows and Linux mkdir python kurs creates the folder python kurs , and cd python kurs changes into it in the terminal. A newly opened terminal is in your home folder; that is where the folder is created. If you have already created it in the editor, you can skip mkdir . In detail Linux, Chapter 2. In the editor, write these three lines and save them as hallo.py in the folder python kurs In the terminal, you change into the folder and start the script by writing the file name after py or python3 Python translates the file, runs the three lines in order and ends; after that, the prompt of the terminal appears again. The second line outputs the value of 2 + 3 , the third outputs the string "2 + 3" literally. In VS Code, the button with the triangle at the top right “Run Python File” runs the same command in the terminal at the bottom of the window. In a script, only print displays anything. This script shows the most important difference from interactive mode The line 2 + 3 is run, but its value appears nowhere. In interactive mode, the same line would have displayed 5 . In a script, only what a call of print outputs appears. Figure 3 abb 3 shows both ways of working side by side. On Windows, the output looks exactly the same. Two ways of working. Left, the interactive mode it reads an input, evaluates it, displays the value and starts over. Right, a script Python translates the whole file and then runs the lines one after another; only what print outputs becomes visible. ⁠ In short A script is a .py file that you run with py datei.py or python3 datei.py ; only what print outputs becomes visible in it. The rule is stated this way in the Python Language Reference if a line is just an expression, its value is displayed in interactive mode; in a script, it is computed and discarded. Technically, the interactive mode translates each input in a separate mode of operation that appends an instruction “display value” at the end; when a script is translated, this instruction is missing. With 2 + 3 , the translator goes even further it computes the line in advance, recognizes that its value is not needed anywhere and leaves it out of the bytecode entirely. The reason for the rule is practical. A program should output exactly what its author wants. If a script with a hundred lines of calculation displayed every intermediate result, the actual result would get lost among them. When trying things out in interactive mode, on the other hand, you want to see every value immediately. The comment A script is read more often than it is written, and after a few weeks, even you no longer know what 500 / 4 6 was supposed to mean. You need room for explanations that do not disturb Python. A comment begins with the character and extends to the end of the line. Python skips it completely. A recipe for pizza dough serves 4 people and needs 500 g of flour and 300 ml of water. For 6 people, you divide each amount by 4, which gives the amount for one person, and multiply it by 6 On Windows py rezept.py , the same output appears. The first three lines are entirely comments. In the last two, the comment comes after the statement Python runs the call of print and skips the rest of the line from on. Good comments say what a number means and why something is calculated, not what is written there anyway. In the example, they state the assumptions and the units, because Python does not know those. With a at the beginning of a line, you can also switch off a line temporarily without deleting it. ⁠ In short A comment begins with , applies up to the end of the line and is there only for humans. During translation, CPython first splits the source code up into its smallest components numbers, names, operators, parentheses, strings. A comment is thrown away in this very first step. It no longer appears in the bytecode, and therefore it costs no time when the program runs, however long it is. A inside a string does not start a comment, because there it belongs to the text print "Nr. 5" outputs Nr. 5 . Everyone who programs makes mistakes. This section distinguishes three kinds of errors and shows when Python notices them and how to read its error messages. The syntax error The first kind of error concerns the form of the source code. An illegible recipe. A cook who comes across an illegible sentence while reading through a recipe does not even start cooking. First, they report which sentence cannot be read. A syntax error is a place in the source code that violates the syntax of the language. Python reports it before any line of the file is run. This follows from the two phases from Subsection 2.4 vom quelltext zur ausfuhrung compiler und interpreter.html stufe 2 4 first the whole file is translated, and with a syntax error, no bytecode is produced that could run. The closing parenthesis is missing in the third line Although the first two lines are free of errors, not even “Zeile 1” German for “line 1” appears. The message consists of four lines the file and line number, the affected line, a ^ character below the place where Python pins down the error, and finally the error type SyntaxError with a description, here that the parenthesis was never closed. Further common syntax errors and their messages | Line | Message and cause | | | | | print "Ende | unterminated string literal The string is never closed. | | print "Hallo" | unmatched ' ' A parenthesis is closed that was never opened. | | print „Hallo“ | invalid character '„' U+201E a typographic instead of a straight quotation mark. | | a line that begins with spaces | IndentationError unexpected indent Spaces at the beginning of a line have a meaning in Python and must not stand there without a reason. | In interactive mode, a syntax error affects only that one input; after that, appears again. ⁠ In short A syntax error violates the form; Python reports it before the start, and no line of the file runs. The syntax of Python allows only the straight quotation mark " and the apostrophe ' as the beginning and end of a string. The curly quotes that a word processor inserts while you type, “ and ” in English or „ and “ in German, are completely different characters for Python. They are allowed inside a string; outside of one, they do not belong to any component of the language. Python therefore rejects a file with the line print „Hallo“ as early as during translation The message names the forbidden character together with its number every written character has a number that is fixed worldwide, and U+201E is the number of the low quotation mark that opens a quotation in German. On the screen, the characters „ and " look similar; the number tells them apart unambiguously. The runtime error Source code can be completely correct in its form and still demand something that cannot be carried out. A missing ingredient. The cook has read the recipe and begins. At step 2, they discover that the eggs are missing. By then, they have already done step 1; they get no further than step 2. A runtime error is an error that occurs only when a line is run. All lines before it have already run; the program aborts at this point. Division by zero is allowed in its form but cannot be carried out This time, “Zeile 1” appears the file was translated without errors, and the first line has run. In the second line, the division fails, the program aborts, and “Zeile 3” never appears. Figure 4 abb 4 contrasts the two cases. Syntax error and runtime error. On the left, an error of form in line 3 prevents even the translation; no line runs. On the right, the translation succeeds, line 1 runs, and the error occurs only when line 2 is run. ⁠ In short A runtime error occurs when a line is run; everything before it has run, nothing after it has. The reason is the two phases of CPython Subsection 2.4 vom quelltext zur ausfuhrung compiler und interpreter.html stufe 2 4 . In the first phase, the translator checks only the form, and it does so for the whole file. Without a valid form, no bytecode is produced, and the second phase does not even begin. Whether a line can actually be run only becomes apparent in the second phase, when the interpreter loop reaches it. This is remarkable in the case of 5 / 0 . The translator does compute fixed numeric expressions such as 2 + 3 in advance Subsection 2.4 vom quelltext zur ausfuhrung compiler und interpreter.html stufe 2 4 , but not the division by zero it deliberately leaves it in the bytecode. Its meaning is defined as “an error occurs when this line is run”. If the translator computed it in advance and failed in doing so, line 1 would not run either, and the program would behave differently from what the semantics prescribes. The exception Python needs a uniform way to report an error and to stop the program at that point. An exception is the event with which Python reports an error. It has a type, for example ZeroDivisionError , and a description, for example division by zero . If it occurs while the program is running, it aborts the program at that point. So a runtime error raises an exception. Python also reports a syntax error as an exception, with the type SyntaxError , only already during translation. Three types of exceptions that occur in this chapter SyntaxError The source code violates the syntax. ZeroDivisionError A division by zero. NameError Python does not know a name. This typically happens when the quotation marks around a text are missing. Without quotation marks, Python takes a word to be a name, as print is one, and looks for something with that name The description sometimes depends on the version. If you divide a number with decimal places by zero, Python 3.13 on Windows reports ZeroDivisionError float division by zero , while Python 3.14 on Linux reports only ZeroDivisionError division by zero . The type stays the same. ⁠ In short An exception reports an error with a type and a description; while the program is running, it aborts the program. The traceback When an exception aborts a program, you want to know what happened, where and why. Python provides a report with a fixed structure for this. The traceback is the report that Python outputs when an exception aborts a program while it is running. It names the place in the source code where the exception occurred and, in its last line, the type and the description of the exception. Figure 5 abb 5 breaks the traceback of laufzeitfehler.py down into its parts. A traceback broken down into its parts Linux; on Windows, line 2 contains the Windows path . You read it from the bottom first the exception 5 , then the location 2 to 4 . You read a traceback from the bottom the last line says what happened, the lines above it say where. In longer programs, there are further location lines above the error location, because the traceback traces the whole path to the error location; the lowest location line is always the place where the exception actually occurred. The marker below the line has existed since Python 3.11. If the error concerns the whole line, Python leaves the marker out. In interactive mode, instead of a file name, there is , counted from the first input; in the simpler earlier version of the interactive mode, it says After the traceback, the interactive mode simply waits for the next input. ⁠ In short A traceback names the location and the type of an exception; you read it from the bottom. The header already says it most recent call last , the most recent step comes last. A traceback is in chronological order. It begins where the program started and ends where it failed. In the programs in this chapter, this path is only one step long. Larger programs consist of parts that call each other; then the traceback lists every part on the way to the error location, and the list becomes long. For finding the error, however, the end of the path is almost always what matters first. That is why you read from the bottom. A practical side effect in the terminal, the output scrolls away upward, and the last lines remain visible. With a long traceback, the most important part is therefore exactly where your eye looks after the program has ended. The logic error Python does not report the most dangerous kind of error at all. The wrong recipe. A cook follows a recipe that says “salt” instead of “sugar”. Every step is readable and can be carried out; the cake even turns out fine, it just does not taste good. A logic error is an error in which a program runs without an error message but does not compute what was intended. If you drive a route at 60 km/h there and at 40 km/h back, your average speed is not 50 km/h but lower on the way back, you are on the road longer, so the slow speed counts for longer. If each direction is 120 km long, the way there takes 2 hours and the way back 3. For 240 km, you then need 5 hours, so on average km/h. In general, the average speed is , where is the speed on the way there and the speed on the way back. Here this gives . In the following script, the parentheses around the denominator are missing Following its rules, Python calculates and is right to do so; something else was intended. The average must lie between the two speeds, that is, between 40 and 60 km/h; 120 km/h cannot be right. With 2 60 40 / 60 + 40 , the result is 48.0 . Further typical logic errors from this chapter a comma instead of a point 2,5 2 gives two values instead of 5.0 Subsection 4.4 der interaktive modus.html stufe 4 4 ; ^ instead of 2 ^ 3 gives 1 instead of 8; a wrong unit a price in euros is labeled “cents”. What helps against it. Check every result with a case whose answer you know, or with a rough estimate. For the average, two equal speeds are suitable if you drive at 50 km/h there and back, your average speed is 50 km/h. The correct formula gives 50, the wrong one 150. ⁠ In short A logic error runs without a message and yields a wrong result; you find it only by checking results. Python checks the form during translation and, while the program runs, whether each line can be run. What the author meant is written nowhere in the source code, so Python cannot check it either. Behind this lies a fundamental limit. Computer science has proven that there can be no method that decides, for every arbitrary program, whether its behavior has a particular property that some programs have and others do not, such as “always outputs the correct average speed”. This is Rice's theorem from 1953. Tools can find many typical errors, but never all of them. Comparing results with known cases therefore remains indispensable. Everything Python calculates with lies in main memory as an object. This section clarifies what an object is, how Python recognizes what you are allowed to do with an object and how you tell two objects apart. The object Chapter 1 /wissen/en/informatik/programmieren/python/programme und der python interpreter/programme und der python interpreter.html called numbers such as 42 and texts such as "Hallo" values Chapter 1, Section 4.2 /wissen/en/informatik/programmieren/python/programme und der python interpreter/der interaktive modus.html stufe 4 2 . While Python works with a value, this value has to be stored somewhere. And Python has to know what kind of value it is you can calculate with the number 42, but not with the text made of the characters 4 and 2. A labeled box. You can picture main memory as a long row of compartments. Python puts each value into a box of its own. On the box, it writes what kind of value lies inside, and each box stands at a fixed place with a place number Fig. 1 abb 1 . This is a picture for orientation how memory is built technically does not matter for what follows. Three objects in main memory, drawn as boxes. Each box carries a label saying what kind of value it contains, and it stands at a fixed place. On the screen, the first and the third number look the same; for Python, they are different things. The place numbers are made up. An object is a piece of main memory in which Python stores a value, together with the information about what kind of value is stored there. Every value Python works with is contained in an object every number, every string, even every intermediate result of a calculation. If you type 42 , 4.0 and "42" one after the other in interactive mode, Python calculates with three objects as in Fig. 1 abb 1 The first contains the integer 42, the second a number with decimal places, the third the text made of the characters 4 and 2. The interactive mode already shows the kind in the notation without a point, with a point, with apostrophes. ⁠ In short An object is a value in main memory that carries the information about its kind with it. The type Before Python combines two values, it has to know what is allowed with them. The plus sign means something different for two numbers than for two texts, and for a number and a text it means nothing at all. The label on the box. In Fig. 1 abb 1 , each box says what kind of value it contains. In Python, this label has a name of its own. The type of an object is the kind of its value. It determines which values the object can have and what you can do with it. The function type returns the type of an object. The three objects from Fig. 1 abb 1 have three different types is Python's way of writing “the type int ”; the word class stands for a type here. The three names are abbreviations | Type | short for | meaning | examples | | | | | | | int | integer | whole number | 42 , 7 , 0 | | float | floating point number | number with decimal places | 4.0 , 0.5 , 2.5e 3 | | str | string | sequence of characters | "42" , 'Regen' | Which type a number gets is decided by its notation alone without a point and without e , it is an int ; with a point or with e , it is a float . That is why 4e3 is also a float , although the value 4000 is a whole number The plus sign shows what the type does. For two objects of type int , it adds; for two objects of type str , it joins the texts together; and for a str and an int , Python knows no rule The exception Chapter 1, Section 6.3 /wissen/en/informatik/programmieren/python/programme und der python interpreter/fehler lesen und verstehen.html stufe 6 3 is of type TypeError . The description gives the reason a str can only be extended by another str , not by an int . So Python does not convert the number 3 into the text "3" on its own. ⁠ In short The type says what kind of value an object contains and what you can do with it; type displays it. Main memory holds nothing but patterns of numbers. The same pattern can mean a number or a sequence of letters, depending on how you read it. That is why, in CPython, every object carries a reference to its type, right at the beginning of its memory area. When the interpreter loop Chapter 1, Section 2.4 /wissen/en/informatik/programmieren/python/programme und der python interpreter/vom quelltext zur ausfuhrung compiler und interpreter.html stufe 2 4 encounters a plus sign, it looks up the type of both values and carries out the addition rule that belongs to these types. If there is no matching rule, it raises a TypeError . In the C language, this is different there, you write down in the source code which type each memory cell has, and the compiler already chooses the matching machine instruction during translation. In the finished program, the type no longer appears anywhere. This makes C faster, because nothing has to be looked up. Python pays for the lookup with time on every calculation and gains flexibility in return the same line of source code can work once with integers, once with floating point numbers and once with text. The identity Two objects can have the same type and the same value and still be two different boxes. To tell them apart, each object needs a mark that only it has. The place number. In Fig. 1 abb 1 , each box stands at a place of its own. You recognize two boxes with the same label and the same content by their different place numbers. The identity of an object is an integer that distinguishes the object from all other objects that exist at the same time. It does not change as long as the object exists. The function id returns it. The identity is a long number that looks random On your computer, other numbers appear, and different ones again the next time Python starts. That does not matter the numerical value never matters, only whether two objects have the same identity. For numbers and strings, moreover, the value of an object stays the same forever. A calculation does not change any existing object. It returns a new object that contains the result 2 + 3 leaves the objects 2 and 3 untouched and returns an object with the value 5. ⁠ In short The identity is the fixed number of an object; id displays it. In CPython, the identity is the address at which the object begins in main memory. Hence the large numbers. Other programs that run Python may assign other numbers; the language only requires that the number is unique and does not change. Unique means unique among the objects that exist at the same time. CPython frees an object that no part of the program needs anymore, and its place can be used for a new object. Two objects that exist one after the other can therefore get the same number. So if you compare identities, you have to make sure that both objects still exist. The method Some abilities of a type do not fit any arithmetic symbol converting a text to capital letters or writing a number as a fraction. For this, every type comes with functions of its own. Functions that belong to the box. A function is a ready made subprogram with a name Chapter 1, Section 4.7 /wissen/en/informatik/programmieren/python/programme und der python interpreter/der interaktive modus.html stufe 4 7 . Some functions are attached to a type like buttons on a device you press them on a particular object, and they work with exactly this object. A method is a function that belongs to a type. You call it for an object by writing a dot, the name of the method and parentheses after the object. The type str has a method upper that returns the text in capital letters. The type float has a method as integer ratio that writes the number as a fraction of numerator and denominator The answer 5, 2 consists of two values in parentheses the numerator 5 and the denominator 2, because . The last input shows that each method belongs to its type a float has no method upper . Python reports this as an AttributeError nothing named upper is attached to the object. The parentheses around 2.5 ensure that Python does not take the dot before the method name for a decimal point. For an integer, you need them without parentheses, Python would read 19. as the beginning of the number . ⁠ In short A method is a function of a type; you call it with objekt.name . Integers are Python's simplest number type. This section shows how large they can become, which arithmetic operators Python knows and how it divides with a whole number result, also with negative numbers. The type int Item counts, scores, page numbers, account numbers many things in everyday life are whole numbers. There, you want to calculate exactly, without any rounding, even when the numbers become very large. Digits, as many as needed. On paper, you write an integer with as many digits as it needs. A three digit number needs three digits, a thirty digit number thirty. Python handles integers in exactly this way. The type int comprises the integers An object of type int has no fixed size it grows as large as the number requires and is limited only by main memory. Adding, subtracting and multiplying two int values always yields the exact result as an int . You write an int as a sequence of digits without a point, negative numbers with a minus sign in front. Long numbers may be structured with underscores 1 000 000 is the same number as 1000000 . has 31 digits and is computed exactly. Even a calculation in which a small number stands between two huge ones loses nothing ⁠ In short An int is an integer of arbitrary size; Python calculates with it exactly. A processor calculates with integers of a fixed size. A common size reaches up to ; the machine instruction cuts off anything beyond that, and the result is wrong. The integer types of the C language have such fixed limits. That is why CPython does not store an int as a single machine number but like a number on paper as a sequence of digits. Only the base is not 10 but . Each “digit” is a number from 0 to and occupies a memory word of its own; the sign is stored separately in front. When a number grows, CPython appends further digits. The arithmetic works like the written arithmetic you learned at school digit by digit with carries, each step with ordinary machine instructions. The price is time an addition of large numbers needs many machine instructions instead of a single one. Python can calculate with arbitrarily large int values. For display, however, it has to convert the number into decimal digits, and for huge numbers this is much more costly than any addition the effort grows considerably faster than the number of digits. An attacker could send a server that reads numbers from texts a number with millions of digits and thus keep it busy for a long time. Since Python 3.11, Python therefore refuses conversions with more than 4300 decimal digits. The vulnerability is publicly described under the identifier CVE 2020 10735. The number has been computed; only the display fails. The message names the way to shift the limit. Conversions into systems with a power of two as the base are exempt, because they are fast. Computers store numbers as sequences of zeros and ones. This section explains the binary system, shows how to convert by hand and with Python, and clarifies which fractions can be written with finitely many digits in the binary system. The positional numeral system To understand how a computer stores numbers, you first have to say precisely what a sequence of digits such as 4705 actually means. Then the same idea can be carried over to bases other than 10. Thousands, hundreds, tens, ones. In 4705, the 4 stands for four thousands, the 7 for seven hundreds, the 0 for no tens and the 5 for five ones. Each position is worth ten times as much as the one to its right. Let be a natural number, the base . In the positional numeral system with base , a sequence of digits with stands for the number The number is called the place value of position . Positions are counted from the right, starting at . In the familiar decimal system, . ⁠ In short In a positional numeral system, each digit is multiplied by the place value of its position, and everything is added up. If several comparison operators stand one after another, such as a < b <= c , the expression is called a chained comparison . It yields True if and only if each of the individual comparisons a < b and b <= c yields True . From tighter to looser binding arithmetic operators, then comparisons, then not , then and , and finally or . So and binds more tightly than or , just as times binds more tightly than plus. This section shows how a script executes lines only if a condition is satisfied, how Python recognizes which lines belong to it and how to choose between several cases. The conditional statement if A script reads in the temperature in a room. It should print a warning only if it is warmer than 23 °C there. A fork in the flow. A flowchart draws the flow of a program a box stands for a statement, a diamond for a question, and the arrows show what comes next. Two arrows lead out of the diamond, one for yes and one for no Fig. 1 abb 1 , left . On the no path, the box with the warning is simply bypassed. Flowcharts of a decision. Left, if if the condition is satisfied, the box below the diamond runs; otherwise it is bypassed. Right, if with else exactly one of the two boxes runs. In both cases, the flow then continues at the same place. A conditional statement has the form if Bedingung Anweisungen The first line is called the header line ; it begins with if and ends with a colon. Below it are one or more statements, indented further than the header line. Python evaluates the condition and determines its truth value Subsection 1.9 bedingungen vergleiche und logische operatoren.html stufe 1 9 . If it is True , Python executes the indented statements; otherwise it skips them. In both cases, execution then continues with the next line that again starts as far to the left as the header line. The script asks for the temperature and checks it “Achtung zu warm” is German for “Caution too warm”, “fertig” for “done” Started twice, once with 24.5 °C and once with 22 °C The last line of the script runs in both cases, because it no longer belongs to the condition. ⁠ In short if Bedingung executes the indented lines below it only if the condition is true. The block and indentation Often several statements depend on the same condition. Python must then recognize where they end and where the script continues for all cases. Like an outline. In an outline, subitems are indented; whatever starts further to the left no longer belongs to them. Python reads indentation in the same way Fig. 2 abb 2 . A block can be recognized by its indentation. The two indented lines blue background belong to the header line above them; the last line again starts as far to the left as the header line and always runs. A block is a sequence of statements that are all indented by the same amount and follow a header line, that is, a line with a colon at the end. It ends before the first line that is indented less. A block may itself contain header lines with their own blocks, indented even further. Four spaces per level are usual; this is what the style guide for Python, PEP 8, recommends. Two statements in the block Blocks in interactive mode. You can enter a block there too. After the header line, Python shows the continuation prompt ... instead of Chapter 1, Section 4.1 /wissen/en/informatik/programmieren/python/programme und der python interpreter/der interaktive modus.html stufe 4 1 . As of Python 3.13, interactive mode indents the next line by four spaces on its own; you only type the statement. An empty line ends the input; only then does the block run. Here the block contains a second header line with its own block, indented more deeply Errors in the indentation. If an indentation is wrong, Python rejects the whole script while translating it, as with any syntax error Chapter 1, Section 6.1 /wissen/en/informatik/programmieren/python/programme und der python interpreter/fehler lesen und verstehen.html stufe 6 1 . If the block after a header line is missing, the message is If a line moves back to a depth that did not exist before, Python finds no block to which it belongs A third message, TabError inconsistent use of tabs and spaces in indentation , appears if a file mixes tabs and spaces in such a way that the meaning would depend on the width of a tab. Good editors insert four spaces when you press the Tab key; then this cannot happen. ⁠ In short The indentation determines which lines belong to a header line; a block ends where a line starts further to the left again. Many languages group a block with braces, C for example with { and } . Without braces, only the first statement belongs to the condition in C, no matter how the lines are indented. In heizung aus ; therefore always runs, even though the indentation claims the opposite. Whoever reads the code sees one grouping, the compiler another, and such errors are hard to find. In Python, this cannot happen there are no braces for blocks, so readers and translator cannot see the grouping differently. The indentation that a good programmer would write anyway is itself the rule. As a side effect, the dispute over where the braces belong disappears, and programs become shorter. When splitting a file into its tokens, CPython turns the indentation into two invisible tokens, “indent” and “dedent”, which play exactly the role of the braces in C. For this, it keeps a stack of indentation depths on which initially only the 0 lies. If a new line is indented more deeply than the top number on the stack, it puts the line's depth on top and produces an “indent”. If the line is indented less deeply, it takes numbers off, producing one “dedent” for each, until the top number equals the new depth. If this depth is not on the stack, that is exactly the error “unindent does not match any outer indentation level”. When the depth is measured, a tab counts up to the next multiple of 8. Because other programs often display a tab four characters wide, Python rejects files whose meaning would depend on this width; that is where the TabError comes from. The alternative else The script should not only warn but, in the other case, confirm that the temperature is right. So there are two paths, and exactly one of them should run. Two paths out of the diamond. In the right flowchart of Fig. 1 abb 1 , each of the two arrows leads to a box of its own; afterward, the paths meet again. If it is True , Python executes the block and then returns to the header line to check the condition again. If it is False , execution continues with the first line after the block. A single execution of the block is called an iteration . The condition is checked before each iteration; if it is already false the first time, the block does not run even once. A loop does not have to execute every iteration completely, and it does not always have to run to the end. This section shows how to leave a loop early or skip an iteration, how to put loops inside one another and how to collect a result in a loop, for example a sum. Breaking out with break A search is supposed to stop as soon as it has found something. The condition of the loop often cannot express this, because whether something has been found is only settled in the middle of the block. Once you have found the key, you stop searching. If you search drawers one after another for a key, you do not open another one after finding it, even if there are drawers left. The statement break in the block of a loop ends this loop immediately. The rest of the block is skipped, as are all further iterations, and the program continues with the first line after the loop. An integer is a prime number if it has no divisor apart from 1 and itself. The script tries the possible divisors one after another; at the first one that divides without a remainder, it breaks off. The condition t t <= n limits the search to divisors up to . That is enough if with , then . So every composite number has a divisor that is at most . For 97, the script checks only to 9 instead of 2 to 96. ⁠ In short break ends a loop immediately, typically after a find. A loop may also have an else block, indented as far as its header line. It runs when the loop ends regularly, that is, for while because the condition became false and for for after the last value, but not when break has ended it. With it, the search for the smallest divisor needs no name of its own for “found” The word else is easily misleading here, because it has nothing to do with the condition of the loop. It is best read as “no break ” the block runs if the search has found nothing. Many programmers do not know this form; a name like teiler with the starting value None is easier to understand for most readers. When you clean the rooms along a hotel hallway, you pass over a room with this sign and continue with the next one. The round does not stop; only this one room is left out. The statement continue in the block of a loop ends only the current iteration. The rest of the block is skipped. A for loop continues with the next value, a while loop with the next check of its condition.
